title: Ratios: The Basics
subtitle: Ratios · Mission 01
tagline: Learn what a {{cyan:ratio}} is — and why {{amber:order matters}}.

slides.headline: You're mixing fruit punch. {{cyan:2 cups of juice}} for every {{amber:1 cup of soda}}. What happens if you switch the amounts?
body: It tastes wrong. Way too fizzy. Not enough fruit.
The *amounts* matter, but so does the *comparison* between them. `2 to 1` is a totally different drink than `1 to 2`.
Today's power-up: `ratios`. A ratio is how you write down that comparison — so the recipe tastes right every single time, whether you're making one cup or twenty.

image.alt: A pitcher of fruit punch next to two measuring cups labeled juice and soda

slides.definition: A `ratio` is a way to {{cyan:compare two or more quantities}} using numbers.
slides.plainWords: It tells you how much of one thing you have compared to another.
slides.analogy: Think of it like a **recipe**. If you're making fruit punch, the ratio tells you how many cups of juice to mix with how many cups of soda — so it tastes right every single time.

image.alt: Three apples and two oranges arranged side by side

slides.headline: 3 apples and 2 oranges — three ways to say the same thing
slides.intro: Every ratio can be written three different ways. All three mean **the exact same thing**: for every 3 apples, there are 2 oranges.

cards.name: WITH THE WORD "TO"
cards.description: Say it out loud with the word `to` between the two numbers.

cards.name: WITH A COLON
cards.description: Put a colon (the two-dot punctuation mark) between the two numbers.

cards.name: AS A FRACTION
cards.description: Write it like a fraction — first number on top, second number on bottom.

image.alt: Three panels showing the same ratio written as 3 to 2, 3:2, and 3/2

slides.headline: Order matters — a lot
slides.intro: The number you write **first** is the thing you're talking about first. Switch the order, and you've written a different ratio entirely.

cards.name: APPLES TO ORANGES
cards.description: If the question asks for `apples to oranges`, write the apples first: {{cyan:3 : 2}}.

cards.name: ORANGES TO APPLES
cards.description: If the question asks for `oranges to apples`, write the oranges first: {{amber:2 : 3}}.

cards.name: READ THE QUESTION CAREFULLY
cards.description: Whichever thing the question names *first* — that's the number that goes first in your ratio.

slides.headline: Part-to-part vs. part-to-whole
slides.intro: Ratios can compare two groups to *each other*, or one group to the *total*. Same math, different question.

cards.name: PART-TO-PART
cards.description: Compares one group to another group.

cards.name: PART-TO-WHOLE
cards.description: Compares one group to the total of everything.

example.label: EXAMPLE
example.text: 3 apples out of 5 pieces of fruit  →  3 : 5

image.alt: Two labeled illustrations — left shows apples and oranges compared to each other, right shows apples compared to the full fruit bowl

slides.headline: Equivalent ratios — same recipe, different batch size
slides.intro: Just like fractions, ratios can be scaled up or down. As long as you {{cyan:multiply or divide both numbers by the same value}}, the relationship stays the same. Same taste, bigger batch.

rows.name: Step 1 — Start with your ratio
rows.description: Write down the ratio you already have. Example: `2 : 1` for one batch of fruit punch (2 cups juice, 1 cup soda).

rows.name: Step 2 — Pick a number to scale by
rows.description: Decide how much bigger or smaller you want the batch to be. Doubling? Pick 2. Tripling? Pick 3. Cutting in half? Pick 2, but you'll divide instead.

rows.name: Step 3 — Do the same thing to *both* numbers
rows.description: Multiply *both* sides by the same number (or divide *both* sides by the same number). Both, always. Never just one.

counter.label: COMMON TRAP
counter.text: Do NOT change only one number. If you double the juice but not the soda, you get a different recipe — not an equivalent ratio.

rows.name: Step 4 — Check the taste
rows.description: The relationship stayed balanced. `2 : 1` doubled becomes `4 : 2`. Tripled: `6 : 3`. All three are `equivalent` — same drink, different batch size.

image.alt: A table showing three batches of fruit punch: single (2:1), double (4:2), and triple (6:3)

prompt.label: QUICK CHECK
prompt.scenario: A fruit bowl has 3 apples and 2 oranges. You want to write the ratio of apples to oranges.
prompt.question: Which of these is **NOT** a correct way to write that ratio?

correct.title: ✓ SPOTTED IT
body: `3 and 2` isn't a ratio — it's just two numbers next to each other. The three real ways to write a ratio are `3 to 2`, `3 : 2`, and `3 / 2`.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** the word `and` doesn't compare — it just lists. Ratios always use `to`, a colon, or fraction form.

a.title: ✕ THAT'S ACTUALLY CORRECT
body: `3 to 2` is one of the three valid ways to write a ratio. Look for the option that *isn't* a ratio at all.

b.title: ✕ THAT'S ACTUALLY CORRECT
body: `3 : 2` (with a colon) is a valid ratio notation. Look for the option that *isn't* a ratio at all.

c.title: ✕ THAT'S ACTUALLY CORRECT
body: `3 / 2` (fraction form) is a valid way to write a ratio. Look for the option that *isn't* a ratio at all.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ RECALIBRATE
body: The three ways to write a ratio are: `3 to 2`, `3 : 2`, and `3 / 2`. Any other format isn't a ratio.

prompt.label: SORTING DRILL
prompt.scenario: Each ratio below compares two things. Some compare one group to another group. Others compare one group to the total.
prompt.question: Drop each ratio into the correct bin.

cards.text: 3 apples out of 5 pieces of fruit
4 red marbles out of 7 total marbles

correct.title: ✓ ALL SORTED
body: You spotted the difference: `part-to-part` compares one group to another, `part-to-whole` compares one group to the total of everything.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** look for the word `out of` — it usually signals `part-to-whole`. The word `to` between two groups usually signals `part-to-part`.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ ONE OR MORE ARE IN THE WRONG BIN
body: Check each card one at a time. If the ratio compares **two different groups**, it's `part-to-part`. If it compares **one group to the total of everything**, it's `part-to-whole`.

prompt.label: PAIR THEM UP
prompt.scenario: Each ratio on the left has an equivalent version on the right — scaled up by multiplying both numbers by the same value.
prompt.question: Match each original ratio to its equivalent.

correct.title: ✓ ALL PAIRED
body: Every pair scaled by the same factor on both sides. `2:1` × 3 = `6:3`. `3:4` × 3 = `9:12`. `5:2` × 2 = `10:4`. `1:3` × 4 = `4:12`. Same recipe, bigger batch.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** to check if two ratios are equivalent, ask *what did I multiply both sides by?* If it's the same number, they're equivalent.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ ONE OR MORE PAIRS ARE OFF
body: For each pair, check: did the *same number* get multiplied on both sides? If the left side was multiplied by 3, the right side has to be multiplied by 3 too. Both sides. Always the same number.

prompt.label: BATCH DRILL
prompt.scenario: Your fruit punch recipe uses `2 cups of juice to 1 cup of soda` (a single batch). You need to make a **triple** batch. Fill in the amounts.
prompt.question: Fill in the missing numbers so the ratio stays equivalent.

blanks.hint: You're tripling the recipe. Multiply the juice amount (2) by 3.
You're tripling the recipe. Multiply the soda amount (1) by 3.

correct.title: ✓ TRIPLE BATCH READY
body: `2 : 1` tripled is `6 : 3`. Six cups of juice, three cups of soda. Same taste as the single batch — just three times as much of it.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** whenever you scale a ratio, do the same thing to both sides. Triple one, triple the other. Every time.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ CHECK BOTH SIDES
body: Triple means multiply by 3. `2 × 3 = 6` for the juice. `1 × 3 = 3` for the soda. So `2 : 1` tripled is `6 : 3`.

prompt.label: CONCEPT CHECK
prompt.scenario: Your friend says: "I don't get why `2:1` and `6:3` are the same. The numbers are totally different!"
prompt.question: Which explanation is the best answer?

options.text: They're the same ratio because we multiplied both sides by 3. The amounts got bigger, but the *comparison* between them stayed the same.
They're the same because 6 and 3 are both bigger than 2 and 1.
They're the same because ratios don't really care about the numbers.
They're not really the same — `6:3` is just a triple batch, so it's a different recipe.

correct.title: ✓ LOCKED IN
body: That's the real answer. A ratio isn't about the amounts — it's about the *comparison*. `2:1` and `6:3` both mean "twice as much juice as soda." The batch got bigger, but the recipe didn't change.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** whenever someone says two ratios are equivalent, ask: *what did they multiply (or divide) both sides by?* If it's the same number, the comparison is unchanged.

b.title: ✕ NOT THE REAL REASON
body: "Bigger" isn't the point. `2:1` and `6:3` are equivalent because both sides got multiplied by the same number (3). If only one side got bigger, they wouldn't be equivalent.

c.title: ✕ RATIOS DEFINITELY CARE ABOUT NUMBERS
body: Ratios care a lot about numbers — specifically, about the *comparison* between them. `2:1` and `6:3` are equivalent because the comparison ("twice as much") is the same in both.

d.title: ✕ ACTUALLY, THEY ARE THE SAME
body: A triple batch has more soup, but the *recipe* is identical. Two cups juice for every one cup soda. `2:1` and `6:3` describe the exact same relationship — just at a different scale.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ RECALIBRATE
body: Two ratios are equivalent when both sides have been multiplied (or divided) by the same number. The amounts change, but the comparison — the recipe — stays the same.

slides.headline: MISSION COMPLETE
slides.subtext: You've got ratios. Comparison, notation, order, types, and scaling — all unlocked.
